facts.claim: Most household microwave ovens operate at 2.45 GHz (2,450 MHz).
spoken: The oven runs at two point four five gigahertz

facts.claim: At 2.45 GHz the wavelength is about 12.2 cm.
spoken: Each wave is about twelve centimetres long

facts.claim: The door window is a thin metal screen with small (millimetre-scale) holes; the glass itself adds little shielding.
facts.caveat: No primary source for an exact hole diameter, so the script says 'tiny' and gives no number
spoken: Behind the glass is a metal screen, full of tiny holes

facts.claim: A metal mesh with holes much smaller than the wavelength blocks (reflects) microwaves like solid metal.
facts.caveat: physics: waveguide below cutoff; FDA: microwaves are reflected by metal
spoken: those tiny holes might as well be solid metal
It bounces off, back into your food

facts.claim: Visible light (0.4-0.7 micrometre wavelength) is far smaller than the holes and passes through.
spoken: Its waves are far smaller than the holes, so they slip right through

facts.claim: US federal standard 21 CFR 1030.10 limits leakage to 5 mW/cm2 at about 2 inches (5 cm) from the oven surface over its lifetime.
facts.caveat: 5 mW/cm2 is the in-service limit; new ovens must be under 1 mW/cm2 before sale. FDA says ~2 in, CFR says 5 cm.
spoken: What little escapes is capped by US law: five milliwatts per square centimetre, two inches from the oven
